claim: Consciousness is thought to be regulated by bidirectional information transfer between the cortex and thalamus.
source: Consciousness is thought to be regulated by bidirectional information transfer between the cortex and thalamus, but the nature of this bidirectional communication - and its possible disruption in unconsciousness - remains poorly understood.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a general premise of the study, representing established scientific thinking.

claim: The nature of bidirectional communication between cortex and thalamus and its possible disruption in unconsciousness remains poorly understood.
source: Consciousness is thought to be regulated by bidirectional information transfer between the cortex and thalamus, but the nature of this bidirectional communication - and its possible disruption in unconsciousness - remains poorly understood.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in current scientific knowledge.

claim: A highly preserved spectral channel of cortical-thalamic communication exists during conscious states.
source: First, we identify a highly preserved spectral channel of cortical-thalamic communication that is present during conscious states, but which is diminished during the loss of consciousness and enhanced during psychedelic states.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by empirical data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The spectral channel of cortical-thalamic communication is diminished during the loss of consciousness.
source: First, we identify a highly preserved spectral channel of cortical-thalamic communication that is present during conscious states, but which is diminished during the loss of consciousness and enhanced during psychedelic states.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by empirical data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The spectral channel of cortical-thalamic communication is enhanced during psychedelic states.
source: First, we identify a highly preserved spectral channel of cortical-thalamic communication that is present during conscious states, but which is diminished during the loss of consciousness and enhanced during psychedelic states.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by empirical data presented in the manuscript.

claim: In humans, mice, and rats, information sent from either the cortex or thalamus via δ/θ/α waves (∼1–13 Hz) is consistently encoded by the other brain region by high γ waves (52–104 Hz).
source: Specifically, we show that in humans, mice, and rats, information sent from either the cortex or thalamus via δ/θ/α waves (∼1–13 Hz) is consistently encoded by the other brain region by high γ waves (52–104 Hz); moreover, unconsciousness induced by propofol anesthesia or generalized spike-and-wave seizures diminishes this cross-frequency communication, whereas the psychedelic 5-methoxy-N,N-dimethyltryptamine (5-MeO-DMT) enhances this low-to-high frequency interregional communication.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by empirical data from multiple species.

claim: Unconsciousness induced by propofol anesthesia diminishes cross-frequency communication between cortex and thalamus.
source: Specifically, we show that in humans, mice, and rats, information sent from either the cortex or thalamus via δ/θ/α waves (∼1–13 Hz) is consistently encoded by the other brain region by high γ waves (52–104 Hz); moreover, unconsciousness induced by propofol anesthesia or generalized spike-and-wave seizures diminishes this cross-frequency communication, whereas the psychedelic 5-methoxy-N,N-dimethyltryptamine (5-MeO-DMT) enhances this low-to-high frequency interregional communication.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by empirical data.

claim: Unconsciousness induced by generalized spike-and-wave seizures diminishes cross-frequency communication between cortex and thalamus.
source: Specifically, we show that in humans, mice, and rats, information sent from either the cortex or thalamus via δ/θ/α waves (∼1–13 Hz) is consistently encoded by the other brain region by high γ waves (52–104 Hz); moreover, unconsciousness induced by propofol anesthesia or generalized spike-and-wave seizures diminishes this cross-frequency communication, whereas the psychedelic 5-methoxy-N,N-dimethyltryptamine (5-MeO-DMT) enhances this low-to-high frequency interregional communication.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by empirical data.

claim: 5-methoxy-N,N-dimethyltryptamine (5-MeO-DMT) enhances low-to-high frequency interregional communication between cortex and thalamus.
source: Specifically, we show that in humans, mice, and rats, information sent from either the cortex or thalamus via δ/θ/α waves (∼1–13 Hz) is consistently encoded by the other brain region by high γ waves (52–104 Hz); moreover, unconsciousness induced by propofol anesthesia or generalized spike-and-wave seizures diminishes this cross-frequency communication, whereas the psychedelic 5-methoxy-N,N-dimethyltryptamine (5-MeO-DMT) enhances this low-to-high frequency interregional communication.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by empirical data.

claim: Changes in cross-frequency cortical-thalamic information transfer may be mediated by excursions of low-frequency thalamocortical electrodynamics toward/away from edge-of-chaos criticality.
source: Second, we leverage numerical simulations and neural electrophysiology recordings from the thalamus and cortex of human patients, rats, and mice to show that these changes in cross-frequency cortical-thalamic information transfer may be mediated by excursions of low-frequency thalamocortical electrodynamics toward/away from edge-of-chaos criticality, or the phase transition from stability to chaos.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by both simulation and empirical data.

claim: Edge-of-chaos criticality is the phase transition from stability to chaos.
source: Second, we leverage numerical simulations and neural electrophysiology recordings from the thalamus and cortex of human patients, rats, and mice to show that these changes in cross-frequency cortical-thalamic information transfer may be mediated by excursions of low-frequency thalamocortical electrodynamics toward/away from edge-of-chaos criticality, or the phase transition from stability to chaos.
evidence: This is a definition provided in the abstract.

claim: The thalamus is among the most important subcortical structures implicated in large-scale neural information processing during normal waking states.
source: Among the subcortical structures that have been implicated in large-scale neural information processing during normal waking states, the thalamus stands out as perhaps the most important (Shine, 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: First-order nuclei of thalamus are the major anatomical bridges across which sensory information is transferred from peripheral sources to the cortex.
source: This is most clearly suggested by its anatomy: the first-order nuclei of thalamus are the major anatomical bridges across which sensory information is transferred from peripheral sources to the cortex, and the presence of extensive connections between higher order thalamic nuclei and diverse cortical regions suggests that these nuclei are among the key bridges through which information is transferred from one part of the cortex to another (Sherman, 2007; Sherman, 2016; Shine, 2021) - a hypothesis which has found support from diverse neuroimaging studies (Saalmann et al., 2012; Theyel et al., 2010; Hwang et al., 2017; Müller et al., 2020).
evidence: This anatomical fact is stated and supported by citations.

claim: Higher order thalamic nuclei are among the key bridges through which information is transferred from one part of the cortex to another.
source: This is most clearly suggested by its anatomy: the first-order nuclei of thalamus are the major anatomical bridges across which sensory information is transferred from peripheral sources to the cortex, and the presence of extensive connections between higher order thalamic nuclei and diverse cortical regions suggests that these nuclei are among the key bridges through which information is transferred from one part of the cortex to another (Sherman, 2007; Sherman, 2016; Shine, 2021) - a hypothesis which has found support from diverse neuroimaging studies (Saalmann et al., 2012; Theyel et al., 2010; Hwang et al., 2017; Müller et al., 2020).
evidence: This hypothesis is stated and supported by multiple citations to neuroimaging studies.

claim: Unconsciousness consistently coincides with disrupted cortical information processing.
source: It is therefore unsurprising that unconsciousness, which consistently coincides with disrupted cortical information processing (Imas et al., 2005; Toker et al., 2022; Sanjari et al., 2021; Schroeder et al., 2016; Hudetz et al., 2020; Ku et al., 2011; Lee et al., 2013; Mäki-Marttunen et al., 2013; Chen et al., 2020), also appears to consistently coincide with disrupted communication between the cortex and thalamus (Zheng et al., 2017; White and Alkire, 2003; Malekmohammadi et al., 2019; Redinbaugh et al., 2020; Bastos et al., 2021; Afrasiabi et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Unconsciousness consistently coincides with disrupted communication between the cortex and thalamus.
source: It is therefore unsurprising that unconsciousness, which consistently coincides with disrupted cortical information processing (Imas et al., 2005; Toker et al., 2022; Sanjari et al., 2021; Schroeder et al., 2016; Hudetz et al., 2020; Ku et al., 2011; Lee et al., 2013; Mäki-Marttunen et al., 2013; Chen et al., 2020), also appears to consistently coincide with disrupted communication between the cortex and thalamus (Zheng et al., 2017; White and Alkire, 2003; Malekmohammadi et al., 2019; Redinbaugh et al., 2020; Bastos et al., 2021; Afrasiabi et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Critical and near-critical systems tend to have a high capacity for transmitting and encoding information.
source: It is by now well-established that critical and near-critical systems tend to have a high capacity for transmitting and encoding information (Langton, 1990; Crutchfield and Young, 1988; Boedecker et al., 2012; Bertschinger and Natschläger, 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Avalanche criticality and edge-of-chaos criticality have been associated with the dynamics of the waking, healthy brain.
source: There are many types of critical points, but in the context of neuroscience, two types of critical points, namely avalanche criticality and edge-of-chaos criticality, may be particularly relevant, as both been associated with the dynamics of the waking, healthy brain (O'Byrne and Jerbi, 2022).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Edge-of-chaos criticality is particularly relevant for supporting information processing in the brain.
source: In this study, we focus exclusively on the edge-of-chaos transition, a critical point that is perhaps particularly relevant for supporting information processing in the brain (O'Byrne and Jerbi, 2022; Toker et al., 2022) and in complex systems more generally (Langton, 1990; Crutchfield and Young, 1988; Boedecker et al., 2012; Bertschinger and Natschläger, 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Slow cortical electrodynamics during conscious states operate near the edge-of-chaos critical point.
source: In our recent work (Toker et al., 2022), we showed that slow cortical electrodynamics during conscious states specifically operate near the edge-of-chaos critical point, or the transition between periodicity and chaos, and that this form of criticality supports the information-richness of waking cortical electrodynamics.
evidence: This statement refers to prior work by the authors and is supported by a citation.

claim: Edge-of-chaos criticality supports the information-richness of waking cortical electrodynamics.
source: In our recent work (Toker et al., 2022), we showed that slow cortical electrodynamics during conscious states specifically operate near the edge-of-chaos critical point, or the transition between periodicity and chaos, and that this form of criticality supports the information-richness of waking cortical electrodynamics.
evidence: This statement refers to prior work by the authors and is supported by a citation.

claim: Slow cortical electrodynamics transition away from edge-of-chaos criticality during anesthesia, generalized seizures, and coma.
source: We also showed that slow cortical electrodynamics transition away from this critical point during anesthesia, generalized seizures, and coma (which diminishes the information-richness of cortical activity), and that slow cortical electrodynamics transition closer to this critical point following the administration of the serotonergic hallucinogen lysergic acid diethylamide (which enhances the information-richness of cortical activity; Toker et al., 2022).
evidence: This statement refers to prior work by the authors and is supported by a citation.

claim: Transitioning away from edge-of-chaos criticality diminishes the information-richness of cortical activity.
source: We also showed that slow cortical electrodynamics transition away from this critical point during anesthesia, generalized seizures, and coma (which diminishes the information-richness of cortical activity), and that slow cortical electrodynamics transition closer to this critical point following the administration of the serotonergic hallucinogen lysergic acid diethylamide (which enhances the information-richness of cortical activity; Toker et al., 2022).
evidence: This statement refers to prior work by the authors and is supported by a citation.

claim: Slow cortical electrodynamics transition closer to edge-of-chaos criticality following administration of lysergic acid diethylamide.
source: We also showed that slow cortical electrodynamics transition away from this critical point during anesthesia, generalized seizures, and coma (which diminishes the information-richness of cortical activity), and that slow cortical electrodynamics transition closer to this critical point following the administration of the serotonergic hallucinogen lysergic acid diethylamide (which enhances the information-richness of cortical activity; Toker et al., 2022).
evidence: This statement refers to prior work by the authors and is supported by a citation.

claim: Transitioning closer to edge-of-chaos criticality enhances the information-richness of cortical activity.
source: We also showed that slow cortical electrodynamics transition away from this critical point during anesthesia, generalized seizures, and coma (which diminishes the information-richness of cortical activity), and that slow cortical electrodynamics transition closer to this critical point following the administration of the serotonergic hallucinogen lysergic acid diethylamide (which enhances the information-richness of cortical activity; Toker et al., 2022).
evidence: This statement refers to prior work by the authors and is supported by a citation.

claim: Cortical activity transitions away from criticality during unconscious states.
source: These results accord with the broad empirical evidence suggesting that cortical activity transitions away from criticality during unconscious states and transitions closer to criticality during psychedelic states (Zimmern, 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Cortical activity transitions closer to criticality during psychedelic states.
source: These results accord with the broad empirical evidence suggesting that cortical activity transitions away from criticality during unconscious states and transitions closer to criticality during psychedelic states (Zimmern, 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Long-range neural communication is likely frequency-multiplexed, with distinct long-range information streams encoded by distinct frequencies of oscillatory neural electrodynamics.
source: Because long-range neural communication is likely frequency-multiplexed, with distinct long-range information streams encoded by distinct (and interacting) frequencies of oscillatry neural electrodynamics (Akam and Kullmann, 2014; Panzeri et al., 2010; Chao et al., 2018; Fontolan et al., 2014; Malekmohammadi et al., 2015), we first evaluated patterns of thalamic-cortical communication during conscious states using a recently developed, spectrally resolved measure of directed information transfer which is both model-free and sensitive to delayed interactions (Pinzuti et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: The ventral posterior thalamic nucleus communicates indirectly with the contralateral somatosensory cortex via its reciprocal connectivity with the ipsilateral somatosensory cortex.
source: Although the recording sites in the GAERS rats are not directly connected, the ventral posterior thalamic nucleus communicates indirectly with the contralateral somatosensory cortex via its reciprocal connectivity with the ipsilateral somatosensory cortex, which directly projects to the contralateral somatosesory cortex (Petreanu et al., 2007; Wise and Jones, 1976; Olavarria et al., 1984).
evidence: This anatomical relationship is stated and supported by citations.

claim: There was significant low-to-high frequency bidirectional cortical-thalamic information transfer across nearly all subjects during conscious states.
source: We found that there was indeed significant low-to-high frequency bidirectional cortical-thalamic information transfer across nearly all subjects during conscious states (Table 1).
evidence: This finding is stated in the text and supported by data presented in Table 1.

claim: Under the null hypothesis, the binomial test returned p=0 for both cortico-thalamic and thalamo-cortical cross-frequency information transfer.
source: To validate the pervasiveness of this phenomenon across subjects, we performed a binomial test treating each subject as a Bernoulli trial with a success being a significant harmonic mean p-value less than 0.05. Under the null hypothesis (i.e., assuming the event of a significant p-value for a subject is a random occurrence with a probability of 0.05), this test returned p=0 for both cortico-thalamic and thalamo-cortical cross-frequency information transfer, confirming that the observed cross-frequency information transfer is a common feature of conscious states across the mammals studied.
evidence: This statistical result is stated in the text.

claim: The observed cross-frequency information transfer is a common feature of conscious states across the mammals studied.
source: To validate the pervasiveness of this phenomenon across subjects, we performed a binomial test treating each subject as a Bernoulli trial with a success being a significant harmonic mean p-value less than 0.05. Under the null hypothesis (i.e., assuming the event of a significant p-value for a subject is a random occurrence with a probability of 0.05), this test returned p=0 for both cortico-thalamic and thalamo-cortical cross-frequency information transfer, confirming that the observed cross-frequency information transfer is a common feature of conscious states across the mammals studied.
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the text and supported by statistical analysis.

claim: Propofol diminished low-frequency to high-frequency information transfer from the cortex to the thalamus in human ET patients (p=0.002).
source: Specifically, propofol diminished low-frequency to high-frequency information transfer from the cortex to the thalamus in both human ET patients (p=0.002, one-tailed Wilcoxon signed-rank test comparing patients' cross-trial medians during waking states versus propofol states) (Figure 3A) and Long-Evans rats (p=0.002; Figure 3B).
evidence: This finding is stated in the text with statistical support and referenced in Figure 3A.

claim: Propofol diminished low-frequency to high-frequency information transfer from the cortex to the thalamus in Long-Evans rats (p=0.002).
source: Specifically, propofol diminished low-frequency to high-frequency information transfer from the cortex to the thalamus in both human ET patients (p=0.002, one-tailed Wilcoxon signed-rank test comparing patients' cross-trial medians during waking states versus propofol states) (Figure 3A) and Long-Evans rats (p=0.002; Figure 3B).
evidence: This finding is stated in the text with statistical support and referenced in Figure 3B.

claim: Cross-frequency corticothalamic information transfer was reduced during generalized spike-and-wave seizures in GAERS rats (p=0.0078).
source: Similarly, cross-frequency corticothalamic information transfer was reduced during generalized spike-and-wave seizures in GAERS rats (p=0.0078; Figure 3C).
evidence: This finding is stated in the text with statistical support and referenced in Figure 3C.

claim: 5-MeO-DMT significantly increased the strength of low-to-high frequency corticothalamic information transfer in C57BL/6 mice (p=0.0312).
source: Conversely, 5-MeO-DMT significantly increased the strength of low-to-high frequency corticothalamic information transfer in C57BL/6 mice (p=0.0312; Figure 3D), despite the fact that this brain state, similar to anesthesia, is marked by reduced high-frequency activity and increased low-frequency activity in both thalamus and cortex (Figure 4); this suggests that these observed changes to cross-frequency communication are independent of the spectral content of thalamocortical electrodynamics.
evidence: This finding is stated in the text with statistical support and referenced in Figure 3D.

claim: The psychedelic brain state induced by 5-MeO-DMT is marked by reduced high-frequency activity and increased low-frequency activity in both thalamus and cortex.
source: Conversely, 5-MeO-DMT significantly increased the strength of low-to-high frequency corticothalamic information transfer in C57BL/6 mice (p=0.0312; Figure 3D), despite the fact that this brain state, similar to anesthesia, is marked by reduced high-frequency activity and increased low-frequency activity in both thalamus and cortex (Figure 4); this suggests that these observed changes to cross-frequency communication are independent of the spectral content of thalamocortical electrodynamics.
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 4.

claim: The observed changes to cross-frequency communication are independent of the spectral content of thalamocortical electrodynamics.
source: Conversely, 5-MeO-DMT significantly increased the strength of low-to-high frequency corticothalamic information transfer in C57BL/6 mice (p=0.0312; Figure 3D), despite the fact that this brain state, similar to anesthesia, is marked by reduced high-frequency activity and increased low-frequency activity in both thalamus and cortex (Figure 4); this suggests that these observed changes to cross-frequency communication are independent of the spectral content of thalamocortical electrodynamics.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that spectral changes are similar in anesthesia and psychedelic states but cross-frequency communication changes differ.

claim: The strength of cross-frequency communication from the thalamus to the cortex was significantly diminished during propofol anesthesia in human ET patients (p=0.002).
source: Specifically, we found that the strength cross-frequency communication from the thalamus to the cortex was significantly diminished during propofol anesthesia in both human ET patients (p=0.002; Figure 5A) and Long-Evans rats (p=0.0098; Figure 5B).
evidence: This finding is stated in the text with statistical support and referenced in Figure 5A.

claim: The strength of cross-frequency communication from the thalamus to the cortex was significantly diminished during propofol anesthesia in Long-Evans rats (p=0.0098).
source: Specifically, we found that the strength cross-frequency communication from the thalamus to the cortex was significantly diminished during propofol anesthesia in both human ET patients (p=0.002; Figure 5A) and Long-Evans rats (p=0.0098; Figure 5B).
evidence: This finding is stated in the text with statistical support and referenced in Figure 5B.

claim: The strength of cross-frequency thalamocortical information transfer was significantly reduced in GAERS rats during generalized spike-and-wave seizures (p=0.0078).
source: Similarly, the strength of cross-frequency thalamocortical information transfer was significantly reduced in GAERS rats during generalized spike-and-wave seizures (p=0.0078; Figure 5C), but did not change during psychedelic states in C57BL/6 mice (p=0.3125; Figure 5D).
evidence: This finding is stated in the text with statistical support and referenced in Figure 5C.

claim: The strength of cross-frequency thalamocortical information transfer did not change during psychedelic states in C57BL/6 mice (p=0.3125).
source: Similarly, the strength of cross-frequency thalamocortical information transfer was significantly reduced in GAERS rats during generalized spike-and-wave seizures (p=0.0078; Figure 5C), but did not change during psychedelic states in C57BL/6 mice (p=0.3125; Figure 5D).
evidence: This finding is stated in the text with statistical support and referenced in Figure 5D.

claim: There was significant variance across brain states in the strength of cross-frequency cortico-thalamic information transfer (p=0.0001), which could not be explained by spectral changes at either low (1–13 Hz) or high (52–104 Hz) frequencies.
source: To confirm that the observed results reflect a breakdown in thalamic-cortical communication rather than changes in the spectral content of thalamocortical electrodynamics, we performed a permutation-based nonparametric analysis of covariance, which revealed significant variance across brain states in the strength of both cross-frequency cortico-thalamic (p=0.0001) and thalamo-cortical (p=0.0001) information transfer, which could not be explained by spectral changes at either low (1–13 Hz) or high (52–104 Hz) frequencies (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This statistical result is stated in the text and supported by analysis in Supplementary file 2.

claim: There was significant variance across brain states in the strength of thalamo-cortical information transfer (p=0.0001), which could not be explained by spectral changes at either low (1–13 Hz) or high (52–104 Hz) frequencies.
source: To confirm that the observed results reflect a breakdown in thalamic-cortical communication rather than changes in the spectral content of thalamocortical electrodynamics, we performed a permutation-based nonparametric analysis of covariance, which revealed significant variance across brain states in the strength of both cross-frequency cortico-thalamic (p=0.0001) and thalamo-cortical (p=0.0001) information transfer, which could not be explained by spectral changes at either low (1–13 Hz) or high (52–104 Hz) frequencies (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This statistical result is stated in the text and supported by analysis in Supplementary file 2.

claim: Non-spectrally resolved transfer entropy between thalamus and cortex did not vary consistently across different brain states.
source: We also confirmed that these observed changes to cross-frequency communication were not driven by changes in non-spectrally resolved information transfer between the thalamus and cortex. Specifically, we found that (non-spectrally resolved) transfer entropy between these two brain regions did not vary consistently across different brain states, instead decreasing significantly during unconsciousness only in human ET patients, and increasing significantly during propofol anesthesia in Long-Evans Rats, generalized spike-and-wave seizures in GAERS rats, and psychedelic states in C57BL/6 mice from both cortex to thalamus (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) and thalamus to cortex (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This finding is stated in the text and supported by data in supplementary figures.

claim: Phase-amplitude coupling between the phase of low-frequency (1–13 Hz) activity in one brain region and the amplitude of high-frequency (52–104 Hz) activity in the other generally increased during propofol anesthesia in Long-Evans Rats, generalized spike-and-wave seizures in GAERS rats, and psychedelic states in C57BL/6 mice.
source: We also found that the observed results were not driven by changes to the strength of phase-amplitude coupling between these regions. Specifically, we found that coupling between the phase of low-frequency (1–13 Hz) activity in one brain region and the amplitude of high-frequency (52–104 Hz) activity in the other, as assessed using the Modulation Index (Tort et al., 2008), generally increased during propofol anesthesia in Long-Evans Rats, generalized spike-and-wave seizures in GAERS rats, and psychedelic states in C57BL/6 mice, with no change during propofol anesthesia in human ET patients from both cortex to thalamus (Figure 3—figure supplement 2) and thalamus to cortex (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This finding is stated in the text and supported by data in supplementary figures.

claim: The strength of low-to-high frequency bidirectional cortical-thalamic information transfer is a specific and novel hallmark of conscious brain states.
source: These results suggest that low-to-high frequency cortical-thalamic information transfer is distinct from both conventional, non-spectral measures of directed information transfer, as well as from conventional measures of cross-frequency coupling, which only take into account linear and same-time interactions. As such, the strength of low-to-high frequency bidirectional cortical-thalamic information transfer is a specific and novel hallmark of conscious brain states.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the comparison of cross-frequency information transfer with other measures.

claim: The mean-field model generated biologically realistic large-scale neural electrodynamics across waking, anesthesia, and spike-and-wave seizure states.
source: Accordingly, we used Bayesian-genetic optimization to tune the parameters of a mean-field model of the basal ganglia-thalamo-cortical system (Figure 6) such that it generated biologically realistic large-scale neural electrodynamics across waking, anesthesia, and spike-and-wave seizure states (see Materials and methods and Figure 6—figure supplements 1–3 for details).
evidence: This is stated in the text and the model is described in Figure 6 and supplementary figures.

claim: Simulated cortical LFPs for the waking state exhibited spectral peaks at all canonical frequency bands, with the strongest peak in the α (8–13 Hz) range.
source: First, our simulated cortical LFPs for the waking state exhibited spectral peaks at all canonical frequency bands, with the strongest peak in the α(8–13 Hz) range (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This finding is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Mean firing rates for each brain region in the model closely matched known region-specific firing rates in mammals.
source: Moreover, mean firing rates for each brain region in the model closely matched known region-specific firing rates in mammals (Table 2).
evidence: This finding is stated in the text and supported by data in Table 2.

claim: There was a significant, positive correlation between fluctuations in the model's cortical firing rate and fluctuations in the amplitude of high-frequency (60–200 Hz) simulated cortical LFP activity (r=0.175, p=1.1e-35).
source: Furthermore, as in the real brain (Ray et al., 2008), there was a significant, positive correlation between fluctuations in our model's cortical firing rate and fluctuations in the amplitude of high-frequency (60–200 Hz) simulated cortical LFP activity (r=0.175, p=1.1e-35).
evidence: This finding is stated in the text with statistical support and compared to empirical data.

claim: At a 100% anesthetic 'dose', simulated cortical LFPs exhibited increased low-frequency power and decreased high-frequency power relative to the simulated LFPs corresponding to the waking state.
source: First, in line with empirical results (Figure 4), at a 100% anesthetic 'dose', our simulated cortical LFPs exhibited increased low-frequency power and decreased high-frequency power relative to the simulated LFPs corresponding to the waking state (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This finding is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: Increasing simulated 'doses' of simulated anesthesia effect recapitulated well-established dose-response trajectories of GABAergic anesthetics, including a continual decline in cortical firing rates.
source: Moreover, increasing simulated 'doses' of simulated anesthesia effect recapitulated well-established dose-response trajectories of GABAergic anesthetics, including a continual decline in cortical firing rates (Bastos et al., 2021; Figure 7—figure supplement 3A) and LFP information-richness (Frohlich et al., 2021; Figure 7—figure supplement 3B), a continual rise in the power of low-frequency activity (Billard et al., 1997; Figure 7—figure supplement 3), and a transition to burst suppression followed by isoelectricity and cessation of firing at very high doses (Ching and Brown, 2014; Figure 7).
evidence: This finding is stated in the text with citations and supported by data in supplementary figures.

claim: Simulated LFPs in the anesthesia state were more strongly chaotic than simulated cortical LFPs in the waking state.
source: Moreover, in line with both prior modeling (Steyn-Ross et al., 2013) and empirical (Toker et al., 2022) work, our simulated LFPs in the anesthesia state were more strongly chaotic than simulated cortical LFPs in the waking state (Figure 7—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This finding is stated in the text with citations and supported by data in supplementary figures.

claim: The simulated anesthesia effect yielded LFPs with increasingly steep spectral slopes.
source: Furthermore, though these features were not explicitly selected for in our parameter optimization, our simulated anesthesia effect yielded several additional biologically realistic features, including the generation of LFPs with increasingly steep spectral slopes (Colombo et al., 2019; Lendner et al., 2020; Figure 7—figure supplement 3E), as well as prolonged inhibitory postsynaptic potentials (IPSPs) at excitatory cortical and thalamic relay cells relative to our waking simulation (Kitamura et al., 2003; Hindriks and van Putten, 2012; Hutt and Longtin, 2010; Noroozbabaee et al., 2021; Figure 7—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This finding is stated in the text with citations and supported by data in supplementary figures.

claim: The simulated anesthesia effect yielded prolonged inhibitory postsynaptic potentials (IPSPs) at excitatory cortical and thalamic relay cells relative to the waking simulation.
source: Furthermore, though these features were not explicitly selected for in our parameter optimization, our simulated anesthesia effect yielded several additional biologically realistic features, including the generation of LFPs with increasingly steep spectral slopes (Colombo et al., 2019; Lendner et al., 2020; Figure 7—figure supplement 3E), as well as prolonged inhibitory postsynaptic potentials (IPSPs) at excitatory cortical and thalamic relay cells relative to our waking simulation (Kitamura et al., 2003; Hindriks and van Putten, 2012; Hutt and Longtin, 2010; Noroozbabaee et al., 2021; Figure 7—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This finding is stated in the text with citations and supported by data in supplementary figures.

claim: The generalized spike-and-wave seizure simulation recapitulated a large rise in cortical firing rates.
source: Finally, our generalized spike-and-wave seizure simulation likewise recapitulated several established biological features of seizures, including a large rise in cortical firing rates (Figure 7—figure supplement 5A; although cortical firing rates in our seizure simulation were considerably higher than in empirical data from GAERS rats Jarre et al., 2017) and a loss in the information-richness of cortical LFPs (Mateos et al., 2018; Figure 7—figure supplement 5B).
evidence: This finding is stated in the text with citations and supported by data in supplementary figures.

claim: The generalized spike-and-wave seizure simulation recapitulated a loss in the information-richness of cortical LFPs.
source: Finally, our generalized spike-and-wave seizure simulation likewise recapitulated several established biological features of seizures, including a large rise in cortical firing rates (Figure 7—figure supplement 5A; although cortical firing rates in our seizure simulation were considerably higher than in empirical data from GAERS rats Jarre et al., 2017) and a loss in the information-richness of cortical LFPs (Mateos et al., 2018; Figure 7—figure supplement 5B).
evidence: This finding is stated in the text with citations and supported by data in supplementary figures.

claim: Simulated LFPs in the seizure state were periodic.
source: In addition, following both prior empirical (Toker et al., 2022) and modeling (Steyn-Ross et al., 2013; Breakspear et al., 2006) results, our simulated LFPs in the seizure state were periodic, that is were insensitive to small perturbations (Figure 7—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This finding is stated in the text with citations and supported by data in supplementary figures.

claim: There was a clear peak of bidirectional, cross-frequency information transfer between simulated cortical and thalamic LFPs when simulated thalamocortical electrodynamics were poised near the edge-of-chaos critical point.
source: Consistent with our predictions, we found that there was a clear peak of bidirectional, cross-frequency information transfer between our simulated cortical and thalamic LFPs when our simulated thalamocortical electrodynamics were poised near the edge-of-chaos critical point (Figure 8A–B).
evidence: This finding is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 8A-B.

claim: Bidirectional cross-frequency information transfer decayed as the simulated anesthetic effect was increased, which generated increasingly chaotic thalamocortical LFPs.
source: We found that bidirectional cross-frequency information transfer decayed as the (simulated) anesthetic effect was increased, which generated increasingly chaotic thalamocortical LFPs; likewise, cross-frequency information transfer between thalamus and cortex decayed as the (simulated) seizure effect was increased, which generated increasingly periodic LFPs, as shown in Figure 8A–B.
evidence: This finding is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 8A-B.

claim: Cross-frequency information transfer between thalamus and cortex decayed as the simulated seizure effect was increased, which generated increasingly periodic LFPs.
source: We found that bidirectional cross-frequency information transfer decayed as the (simulated) anesthetic effect was increased, which generated increasingly chaotic thalamocortical LFPs; likewise, cross-frequency information transfer between thalamus and cortex decayed as the (simulated) seizure effect was increased, which generated increasingly periodic LFPs, as shown in Figure 8A–B.
evidence: This finding is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 8A-B.

claim: The K-statistic of the modified 0–1 chaos test was significantly correlated with the estimated largest Lyapunov exponent of simulated LFPs (ρ=0.76, p=0).
source: Indeed, when applied to simulated thalamocortical LFPs bandpass filtered between 1–13 Hz (matching the slow frequencies of cortical-thalamic information transfer identified here), the K-statistic was significantly correlated with the estimated largest Lyapunov exponent of our simulated LFPs (ρ=0.76, p=0), and could moreover recapitulate the observed relationship between thalamocortical chaoticity and cross-frequency cortical-thalamic information transfer in our mean-field model, as shown in Figure 8C–D.
evidence: This finding is stated in the text with statistical support and referenced in Figure 8C-D.

claim: The K-statistic of the modified 0–1 chaos test can be used to test the predicted relationship between proximity to edge-of-chaos criticality and the strength of cross-frequency cortical-thalamic information transfer in real brain data.
source: This indicates that the K-statistic of the modified 0–1 chaos test can be used to test the predicted relationship between proximity to edge-of-chaos criticality and the strength of cross-frequency cortical-thalamic information transfer in real brain data.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the validation of the K-statistic in simulations.

claim: GABAergic anesthesia destabilized slow thalamocortical electrodynamics in humans (p=0.065).
source: Importantly, replicating both prior simulation and empirical results (Toker et al., 2022) as well as the novel simulation results presented above (Figure 8, Figure 7—figure supplement 3), we found that GABAergic anesthesia destabilized slow thalamocortical electrodynamics in both humans (p=0.065, one-tailed Wilcoxon signed-rank test comparing patients' cross-trial median K-statistic during waking states versus propofol anesthesia states) and rats (p=0.002, one-tailed Wilcoxon signed-rank test).
evidence: This finding is stated in the text with statistical support and citations.

claim: GABAergic anesthesia destabilized slow thalamocortical electrodynamics in rats (p=0.002).
source: Importantly, replicating both prior simulation and empirical results (Toker et al., 2022) as well as the novel simulation results presented above (Figure 8, Figure 7—figure supplement 3), we found that GABAergic anesthesia destabilized slow thalamocortical electrodynamics in both humans (p=0.065, one-tailed Wilcoxon signed-rank test comparing patients' cross-trial median K-statistic during waking states versus propofol anesthesia states) and rats (p=0.002, one-tailed Wilcoxon signed-rank test).
evidence: This finding is stated in the text with statistical support and citations.

claim: Slow thalamocortical activity became periodic or hyper-stable during generalized spike-and-wave seizures (p=0.0078).
source: Conversely, slow thalamocortical activity became periodic or hyper-stable during generalized spike-and-wave seizures (p=0.0078, one-tailed Wilcoxon signed-rank test).
evidence: This finding is stated in the text with statistical support.

claim: 5-MeO-DMT moderately stabilized cortical electrodynamics (p=0.0312).
source: Finally, 5-MeO-DMT moderately stabilized cortical electrodynamics (p=0.0312, one-tailed Wilcoxon signed-rank test), which is consistent with prior results showing that psychedelics tune slow neural electrodynamics closer to edge-of-chaos criticality, and do so by approaching the critical point from the chaotic side of the edge (Toker et al., 2022).
evidence: This finding is stated in the text with statistical support and citations.

claim: The estimated chaoticity of low-frequency (1–13 Hz) thalamocortical electrodynamics varied significantly across brain states (p=0.0001).
source: Finally, while the estimated chaoticity of low-frequency (1–13 Hz) thalamocortical electrodynamics varied significantly across brain states (p=0.0001) as assesed by permutation-based nonparametric ANCOVA (Scheiner and Gurevitch, 2001), this variance could not be explained by changes to spectral power in this frequency range in the thalamocortical system across brain states (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This finding is stated in the text with statistical support.

claim: The variance in estimated chaoticity of low-frequency thalamocortical electrodynamics across brain states could not be explained by changes to spectral power in this frequency range.
source: Finally, while the estimated chaoticity of low-frequency (1–13 Hz) thalamocortical electrodynamics varied significantly across brain states (p=0.0001) as assesed by permutation-based nonparametric ANCOVA (Scheiner and Gurevitch, 2001), this variance could not be explained by changes to spectral power in this frequency range in the thalamocortical system across brain states (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This finding is stated in the text with statistical support.

claim: This work is the first to show that edge-of-chaos criticality supports interregional communication in the brain.
source: To our knowledge, this work is the first to show that this precise form of criticality supports interregional communication in the brain.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the work.

claim: The precise code of cross-frequency communication remains to be determined.
source: Although both our empirical and simulated thalamocortical electrodynamics show clear evidence of cross-frequency cortical-thalamic information transfer, and that the strength of this cross-frequency information transfer is supported by the proximity of thalamocortical electrodynamics to edge-of-chaos criticality, much work remains to be done to explain this frequency-specific communication pattern during conscious states. In other words, the precise code of cross-frequency communication remains to be determined.
evidence: This statement identifies a limitation and future direction.

claim: Cross-frequency cortical-thalamic information transfer may be related to the modulation of the amplitude of high-frequency activity by the phase of low-frequency activity.
source: It is possible, for example, that this code will be related to mechanisms that are by now well-established in the neuroscience literature, such as the modulation of the amplitude of high-frequency activity by the phase of low-frequency activity (Canolty and Knight, 2010).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about possible mechanisms.

claim: The observation of cross-frequency information transfer between thalamus and cortex is consistent with prior evidence of low-to-high frequency phase-amplitude coupling between these regions during waking states.
source: Indeed, our observation of cross-frequency information transfer between thalamus and cortex is, at least conceptually, consistent with prior evidence of low-to-high frequency phase-amplitude coupling between these regions during waking states (Fitzgerald et al., 2013; Malekmohammadi et al., 2019; Opri et al., 2019; Malekmohammadi et al., 2015); however, it is important to note that, unlike the strength of directed cross-frequency information transfer, the strength of phase-amplitude coupling did not consistently vary as a function of brain state (Figure 3—figure supplement 2, Figure 5—figure supplement 2), which suggests that these are somewhat distinct phenomena.
evidence: This statement compares the current findings with prior research and is supported by citations.

claim: The strength of phase-amplitude coupling did not consistently vary as a function of brain state, suggesting that cross-frequency information transfer and phase-amplitude coupling are somewhat distinct phenomena.
source: Indeed, our observation of cross-frequency information transfer between thalamus and cortex is, at least conceptually, consistent with prior evidence of low-to-high frequency phase-amplitude coupling between these regions during waking states (Fitzgerald et al., 2013; Malekmohammadi et al., 2019; Opri et al., 2019; Malekmohammadi et al., 2015); however, it is important to note that, unlike the strength of directed cross-frequency information transfer, the strength of phase-amplitude coupling did not consistently vary as a function of brain state (Figure 3—figure supplement 2, Figure 5—figure supplement 2), which suggests that these are somewhat distinct phenomena.
evidence: This inference is drawn from comparing the behavior of two different measures across brain states.

claim: The model is the first to encapsulate cross-frequency information transfer between the thalamus and cortex in the context of simulating the waking brain.
source: In the context of simulating the waking brain, our model is the first to encapsulate cross-frequency information transfer between the thalamus and cortex, a phenomenon our empirical data and analyses have uniquely identified.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the model.

claim: Prior models of the full basal ganglia-thalamo-cortical system during healthy, waking states have largely relied on the assumption that neural dynamics in these states are typified by a stable fixed point possibly perturbed by noise.
source: Moreover, prior models of the full basal ganglia-thalamo-cortical system during healthy, waking states have largely relied on the assumption that neural dynamics in these states are typified by a stable fixed point (possibly) perturbed by noise (van Albada and Robinson, 2009; Holgado et al., 2010; Pavlides et al., 2012) - an assumption not supported by our current (Supplementary file 5) or prior (Toker et al., 2022) findings, and our model, which generates nonlinear oscillatory behavior, accords with these findings.
evidence: This statement characterizes prior modeling approaches and is supported by citations.

claim: The assumption that neural dynamics in waking states are typified by a stable fixed point is not supported by current or prior findings.
source: Moreover, prior models of the full basal ganglia-thalamo-cortical system during healthy, waking states have largely relied on the assumption that neural dynamics in these states are typified by a stable fixed point (possibly) perturbed by noise (van Albada and Robinson, 2009; Holgado et al., 2010; Pavlides et al., 2012) - an assumption not supported by our current (Supplementary file 5) or prior (Toker et al., 2022) findings, and our model, which generates nonlinear oscillatory behavior, accords with these findings.
evidence: This statement is supported by references to current and prior findings.

claim: The model is the first to accurately recapitulate waking state firing rates in the cortex and all major subcortical areas while also generating oscillatory dynamics in the regime of weak chaos, near edge-of-chaos criticality.
source: Our model of the full basal ganglia-thalamo-cortical system is also the first, to our knowledge, to accurately recapitulate waking state firing rates in the cortex and all major subcortical areas (Table 2), while also generating oscillatory dynamics in the regime of weak chaos, near edge-of-chaos criticality.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the model and is supported by data in Table 2.

claim: The mean-field model of the basal ganglia-thalamo-cortical system is unique in its inclusion of pallido-thalamic, pallido-cortical, and pallido-striatal projections.
source: Finally, our mean-field model of the basal ganglia-thalamo-cortical system is also unique in its inclusion of pallido-thalamic, pallido-cortical, and pallido-striatal projections (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the model.

claim: The model is the first to associate the emergence of alpha oscillations with Hopf bifurcations specifically in the proximity of edge-of-chaos criticality.
source: Additionally, while prior models have associated the emergence of alpha oscillations with Hopf bifurcations (Grimbert and Faugeras, 2006; Spiegler et al., 2010), our model is the first (to our knowledge) to do so specifically in the proximity of edge-of-chaos criticality.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the model and is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Prior mean-field models of neural electrodynamics during the anesthetized state have largely focused on either just cortical or just thalamo-cortical dynamics.
source: In the context of anesthesia simulations, our model is unique in its inclusion of the basal ganglia, as prior mean-field models of neural electrodynamics during the anesthetized state have largely focused on either just cortical (Steyn-Ross et al., 2013; Kuhlmann et al., 2016; Bojak and Liley, 2005; Liley and Walsh, 2013; Molaee-Ardekani et al., 2007) or just thalamo-cortical dynamics (Ching and Brown, 2014; Hindriks and van Putten, 2012; Noroozbabaee et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement characterizes prior modeling approaches and is supported by citations.

claim: Strong chaos has been identified in cortical-only models of anesthesia.
source: Similarly, while strong chaos has been identified in cortical-only models of anesthesia (Steyn-Ross et al., 2013), our model seeks to offer a broader perspective by introducing this phenomenon in a context that incorporates several subcortical structures.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: It is currently unclear whether information transmission along other frequency bands likewise signposts consciousness.
source: First, although our evidence suggests that cortical-thalamic information transfer from ∼1–13 Hz to 52–104 Hz is a hallmark of conscious brain states, it is currently unclear whether information transmission along other frequency bands likewise signposts consciousness.
evidence: This statement identifies a limitation and area for future research.

claim: Communication from the cortex to the thalamus may be more broadband than thalamus-to-cortex communication.
source: Indeed, in our preliminary exploratory sweep of patterns of information flow (Figure 2), we found that although thalamus-to-cortex communication may be uniquely characterized by this spectral pattern, communication from the cortex to the thalamus may be more broadband.
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 2.

claim: Varying degrees of chaoticity can only be detected with some certainty in simulations.
source: We also stress that currently, varying degrees of chaoticity - and therefore proximity to edge-of-chaos criticality - can only be detected with some certainty in simulations.
evidence: This statement identifies a limitation of current methods.

claim: The modified 0–1 chaos test is a relatively robust method for chaos detection.
source: The modified 0–1 chaos test, which we used here as an empirical test of chaoticity, is a relatively robust method for chaos detection (Toker et al., 2020), correlates well with ground-truth chaoticity in our mean-field model, and reproduces the relationship between chaoticity and cross-frequency cortical-thalamic information transfer observed in our simulations; but, the test's results may be affected by features of a signal, such as noise, which are unrelated to ground-truth chaoticity.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work and validation in the current study.

claim: The results of the modified 0–1 chaos test may be affected by features of a signal, such as noise, which are unrelated to ground-truth chaoticity.
source: The modified 0–1 chaos test, which we used here as an empirical test of chaoticity, is a relatively robust method for chaos detection (Toker et al., 2020), correlates well with ground-truth chaoticity in our mean-field model, and reproduces the relationship between chaoticity and cross-frequency cortical-thalamic information transfer observed in our simulations; but, the test's results may be affected by features of a signal, such as noise, which are unrelated to ground-truth chaoticity.
evidence: This statement identifies a limitation of the method.
